clinicalPearls: Characterised by deep sterile collections of neutrophils that mimic pyogenic abscesses but yield no organisms on culture and fail to respond to antibiotics, yet melt away with corticosteroids.
The spleen is the most frequently affected organ, followed by abdominal and mediastinal lymph nodes, liver, lung and other viscera; lesions are often multiple.
Presents with swinging fever, abdominal pain and profound elevation of inflammatory markers with a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis, closely simulating sepsis.
Strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn disease, and overlaps with the neutrophilic dermatoses such as pyoderma gangrenosum and Sweet syndrome.
Repeatedly negative cultures, negative serology and no response to broad-spectrum antimicrobials are the diagnostic hallmark that should prompt reconsideration of an autoinflammatory cause.
Dramatic and rapid defervescence with corticosteroids is both therapeutic and strongly supportive of the diagnosis.
Relapse on steroid withdrawal is frequent, so steroid-sparing immunosuppressants or biologics are often needed for maintenance.
Considered part of the neutrophilic disease spectrum and by some an autoinflammatory disorder, not an infection despite the abscess morphology.
reference.pathophysiology: Aseptic abscess syndrome is a neutrophilic disorder in which dysregulated innate immunity drives the accumulation of large numbers of neutrophils into focal tissue collections that organise as abscesses but remain sterile. It sits within the broader family of neutrophilic diseases alongside pyoderma gangrenosum, Sweet syndrome and the neutrophilic manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease, and is increasingly regarded as having an autoinflammatory basis with excessive activation of neutrophil recruitment and the innate immune signalling that governs it. Rather than responding to an invading pathogen, neutrophils are drawn into deep organs, most notably the spleen, by aberrant chemotactic and cytokine signals, forming necrotic-appearing collections with a rim of inflammatory tissue. Histology shows a dense neutrophilic infiltrate with central necrosis but no microorganisms on special stains or culture. The frequent coexistence with Crohn disease, relapsing polychondritis and other immune-mediated conditions, together with the shared responsiveness to corticosteroids and neutrophil-directed immunosuppression, points to a common pathway of neutrophil-driven sterile inflammation. The abscesses are therefore an immunological phenomenon; antibiotics are ineffective because there is no infection to treat, and immunomodulation is required to switch off the aberrant neutrophil response.
additionalDifferentials: Pyogenic visceral abscess from bacterial infection
Disseminated tuberculosis or fungal infection with splenic microabscesses
Lymphoma or metastatic malignancy with necrotic deposits
Systemic vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Inflammatory bowel disease with extraintestinal neutrophilic complications
Other neutrophilic dermatoses with systemic involvement including Sweet syndrome
Autoinflammatory syndromes presenting with sterile inflammation
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging of chest, abdomen and pelvis to map the number and distribution of lesions
Repeated aspiration or biopsy of a lesion for microbiology, mycobacterial and fungal culture plus histology
Comprehensive infective screen and serology to exclude occult infection
Inflammatory markers and full blood count showing neutrophilia
Ileocolonoscopy and gut imaging to evaluate for inflammatory bowel disease
Autoimmune and vasculitis serology to exclude mimics
Assessment of therapeutic response to a corticosteroid trial once infection is excluded
redFlags: Failure to exclude genuine infection before starting immunosuppression, risking fulminant sepsis
Haemodynamic instability or features of splenic rupture from a large splenic collection
Rapidly enlarging or numerous lesions with systemic toxicity
Emergence of an underlying malignancy or evolving inflammatory bowel disease during follow-up
Relapse or dissemination when corticosteroids are tapered too quickly
reference.prognosis: The syndrome usually responds rapidly and completely to corticosteroids with resolution of both symptoms and lesions, but relapse on withdrawal is frequent and many patients require prolonged steroid-sparing immunosuppression. Long-term outlook is shaped chiefly by the associated inflammatory bowel or systemic disease.
pitfalls: Persisting with escalating antibiotics for presumed pyogenic abscesses despite repeatedly sterile cultures and no clinical response.
Starting immunosuppression before infection, especially tuberculosis, has been rigorously excluded.
Missing an underlying or subclinical inflammatory bowel disease that requires directed treatment.
Interpreting the abscess morphology as proof of infection rather than sterile neutrophilic inflammation.
Tapering corticosteroids too rapidly and precipitating relapse with new visceral collections.
references: Standard rheumatology and autoinflammatory disease reference texts
Neutrophilic dermatoses and dermatology reference texts
management: Systemic corticosteroids as first-line therapy, typically producing rapid defervescence and resolution of the sterile collections
Steroid-sparing immunosuppression, such as azathioprine or an anti-TNF biologic, to maintain remission and enable steroid withdrawal in relapsing disease
Exclusion of infection with repeated cultures and lesion biopsy before committing to immunosuppression, given the close mimicry of pyogenic abscess and sepsis
Investigation for and treatment of associated inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn disease, and coexisting neutrophilic dermatoses
Surveillance for relapse during steroid tapering, monitoring symptoms, inflammatory markers and cross-sectional imaging of the affected viscera
Multidisciplinary management involving rheumatology and gastroenterology, with drainage reserved for diagnostic sampling rather than definitive treatment
